headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Nutritional Assessment
headings.content: A nutritional assessment is a comprehensive evaluation used to gather and interpret clinical, dietary, biochemical, and anthropometric data. Nurses perform this evaluation to identify malnutrition, whether undernutrition or overnutrition, and to establish a baseline for patient care. Without a structured assessment, subtle nutrient deficiencies can easily go unnoticed until they severely impact a patient's recovery. The main goal is to catch nutritional problems early, allowing the healthcare team to plan effective dietary interventions and improve overall health outcomes.

headings.title: The ABCD Approach to Nutritional Data
headings.content:
To make the evaluation systematic, nurses and dietitians use the ABCD framework. Each letter represents a distinct category of data collection:

- **Anthropometric measurements**: Physical dimensions like height, weight, body mass index, and skinfold thickness.
- **Biochemical data**: Laboratory values such as serum albumin, prealbumin, and electrolyte panels.
- **Clinical examination**: Physical signs of nutrition status visible on the skin, hair, eyes, and oral cavity.
- **Dietary history**: Records of what the patient eats, including recent appetite changes, food allergies, and cultural preferences.

headings.title: Identifying Malnutrition and Nutritional Risk
headings.content: Malnutrition includes both inadequate intake leading to wasting and excessive intake leading to obesity. Nurses must actively screen for risk factors such as involuntary weight loss, chronic illness, swallowing difficulties, and prolonged hospital stays. A common clinical mistake is assuming that only thin patients are malnourished. Patients with chronic conditions or obesity can also suffer from severe micronutrient deficiencies and protein-energy malnutrition.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Screening and Monitoring
headings.content: Screening is the first step, usually performed within twenty-four hours of admission to flag patients who need a full assessment. Nurses are on the front lines of this process because they record daily meal consumption, monitor weight trends, and observe physical changes. When a screening tool indicates high risk, the nurse collaborates with dietitians and physicians to formulate a nutrition care plan and monitor its effectiveness over time.

headings.title: Clinical Significance and Impact on Patient Outcomes
headings.content: Good nutritional status directly supports wound healing, immune function, and muscle strength. Conversely, untreated malnutrition prolongs hospital stays, increases the risk of pressure injuries, and raises infection rates. By prioritizing nutritional assessments, nursing teams help reduce healthcare costs and improve recovery times. Recognizing these links ensures nutrition is treated as a vital clinical vital sign rather than a secondary concern.
